## World models learn by predicting what happens next

Five new papers push robot and game models from perceiving a scene to forecasting it at several horizons, then using the forecast to pick actions.

Five papers in a preprint point in the same direction: a model that acts in the world should first predict how the world will change. World action models learn latent variables from observations and use them both to predict how a scene evolves and to generate actions, so prediction and action are two outputs of one model rather than two separate systems.

The papers differ in what they fix, but they share a diagnosis of the current gap. Existing methods model short-term dynamics and long-term task objectives separately, according to the HiFOR authors, which leaves a disconnect between what happens next and what the task ultimately requires. Standard world action models have a second weakness: they do not guarantee that actions are generated solely from action-relevant latent variables, and may entangle those variables with nuisance variables that prediction happens to use.

HiFOR, a hierarchical foresight framework for robotic manipulation, predicts at three levels at once: short-term state evolution, semantic milestones along the way, and final goal states. A Hierarchical Dependency Mask establishes dependencies across those temporal horizons, so the near-term forecast and the distant goal are not produced independently.
